questions.question: What is the truth value of (p ∨ q) when p = False and q = True?

explanations.a: Correct! The OR operator (∨) is true when at least one of the operands is true. Since q is true, the entire expression (p ∨ q) evaluates to true, regardless of p being false.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The OR operator is false only when both operands are false.
explanations.c: Incorrect. With the given values of p and q, we can definitively determine the truth value.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A logical expression has exactly one truth value for any given assignment.

questions.question: Which formula is logically equivalent to ¬(p ∨ q)?

explanations.a: Correct! This is De Morgan's Law: ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ (¬p ∧ ¬q). The negation of a disjunction becomes a conjunction of the negated components. You can verify this by constructing truth tables for both formulas.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This represents 'not p OR not q', which is different from the negation of 'p OR q'.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This is not equivalent to ¬(p ∨ q).
explanations.d: Incorrect. This formula is not logically equivalent to ¬(p ∨ q).

questions.question: In a truth table for three variables (p, q, r), how many rows represent assignments where exactly two variables are true?

explanations.a: Incorrect. There are more than 2 ways to choose exactly 2 variables out of 3 to be true.
explanations.b: Correct! With three variables, there are exactly 3 ways to have exactly two variables true: (T,T,F), (T,F,T), and (F,T,T). This follows the combination formula C(3,2) = 3.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Four would be the number of rows with exactly one variable true or exactly three variables true.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Six exceeds the number of possible combinations.

questions.question: What is the truth value of (p → q) when p = True and q = False?

explanations.a: Incorrect. This is the one case where an implication is false.
explanations.b: Correct! An implication (p → q) is false only when the antecedent (p) is true and the consequent (q) is false. This represents a 'broken promise' - if p is true, then q should also be true for the implication to hold.
explanations.c: Incorrect. With the given truth values, the result is definitively determined.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The truth value of (p → q) depends only on the values of p and q.

questions.question: Which formula represents the contrapositive of (p → q)?

explanations.a: Incorrect. This is the converse of (p → q), not the contrapositive.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This is the inverse of (p → q), not the contrapositive.
explanations.c: Correct! The contrapositive of (p → q) is (¬q → ¬p). The contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original implication and is formed by negating both parts and switching their order.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This is the negation of the entire implication, not the contrapositive.

questions.question: A formula that is always false regardless of truth assignments is called:

explanations.a: Incorrect. A tautology is a formula that is always true.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A contingency is a formula that is sometimes true and sometimes false.
explanations.c: Correct! A contradiction (also called an unsatisfiable formula) is a formula that evaluates to false under every possible truth assignment. For example, (p ∧ ¬p) is always false regardless of the value of p.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A satisfiable formula has at least one assignment that makes it true.

questions.question: Consider the formula (p ∧ q ∧ r) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q ∧ ¬r). This formula is:

explanations.a: Incorrect. The formula is not true for all assignments (e.g., when p=T, q=T, r=F).
explanations.b: Incorrect. The formula is true when all variables are true or when all variables are false.
explanations.c: Correct! This formula is true in exactly 2 out of 8 possible assignments: when (p,q,r) = (T,T,T) or when (p,q,r) = (F,F,F). For all other combinations, the formula evaluates to false. This makes it a contingency.
explanations.d: Incorrect. These formulas have different truth tables and are not equivalent.

questions.question: Which of the following formulas is unsatisfiable?

explanations.a: Incorrect. This formula simplifies to q and is satisfiable when q = true.
explanations.b: Correct! This formula is unsatisfiable. From (p ∧ q), both p and q must be true. But (¬p ∨ ¬q) requires at least one of them to be false. These two constraints are contradictory, so no truth assignment can satisfy both simultaneously.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This formula is satisfiable when p = false, q = false, and r = true.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This formula is satisfiable when p = true and q = true.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the relationship between satisfiability and validity?

answers.a: Every valid formula is satisfiable, but not every satisfiable formula is valid
answers.b: Every satisfiable formula is valid, but not every valid formula is satisfiable
answers.c: A formula is valid if and only if it is satisfiable
answers.d: Satisfiable and valid formulas are completely unrelated concepts

explanations.a: Correct! A valid (tautology) formula is true under every truth assignment, which means it is definitely satisfiable (satisfied by all assignments). However, a satisfiable formula only needs to be true under at least one assignment—it could be false in other assignments, making it contingent rather than valid. For example, (p ∨ q) is satisfiable (true when p=T or q=T) but not valid (false when p=F and q=F).
explanations.b: Incorrect. Many satisfiable formulas are not valid. For instance, (p ∧ q) is satisfiable but not valid since it's false when either p or q is false.
explanations.c: Incorrect. These are different concepts. While all valid formulas are satisfiable, the converse is not true.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Satisfiability and validity are closely related through the satisfiability hierarchy.
